title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
statement: There are n cities and flights[i] = [from, to, price] describing one-way flights. Return the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops, or -1 if no such route exists.
realWorld: Fare search with a layover limit, and the same shape as routing a packet under a hop-count cap or planning a supply chain with a bounded number of transfers. The constraint is what makes it interesting: the cheapest route and the cheapest route within a budget of hops are frequently different routes.

examples.explanation: 0 -> 1 -> 2 costs 200 and uses one stop, which is allowed.
With no stops allowed only the direct flight qualifies, even though it is more than twice the price. This is the case that breaks plain Dijkstra.
Flights are one-way; there is no route from 0 to 1.

constraints: 0 <= src, dst, from, to < n, src != dst

bruteForce.idea: DFS every route from src, tracking cost and stops, pruning when the stop budget runs out, and keep the cheapest that reaches dst.
code: public static int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
for (int[] flight : flights) adj.get(flight[0]).add(new int[] {flight[1], flight[2]});
private static void search(int city, int dst, int cost, int stopsLeft, List<List<int[]>> adj, int[] best) {
if (city == dst) { best[0] = Math.min(best[0], cost); return; }
search(flight[0], dst, cost + flight[1], stopsLeft - 1, adj, best);

complexity.time: O(n^k) — every city can branch to every other at each of k+1 levels

bruteForce.whySlow: The search tree branches by the out-degree at every level, so the same city is re-expanded once for each distinct route that reaches it — and cost is recomputed from scratch every time. With n = 100 and k near n this is astronomically large, despite there being only 100 cities.

patternIdentification: It looks like Dijkstra, and the trap is that plain Dijkstra is wrong here. Dijkstra settles a city once, at its globally cheapest price — but the cheapest way to reach a city may use too many stops, and a pricier route with fewer stops might be the only one that can still complete the journey. The stop count is a second dimension of the state. Two correct readings follow: Bellman-Ford limited to k+1 relaxation rounds (round r computes the best cost using at most r flights), or Dijkstra over the state (city, stopsUsed) rather than city alone.

optimized.idea: Bellman-Ford with exactly k+1 rounds — k stops means at most k+1 flights. Each round relaxes every flight once, reading from the previous round's array and writing into a copy, so a single round can never chain two flights together. After k+1 rounds the array holds the cheapest cost reachable within the flight budget.
code: public static int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
// k stops == at most k + 1 flights, so k + 1 rounds of relaxation.
// Copy first: relaxing in place would let two flights be used in one
// round, silently exceeding the stop budget.
int from = flight[0], to = flight[1], price = flight[2];
if (cost[from] == Integer.MAX_VALUE) continue;     // no route yet
* Dijkstra variant: the state is (city, flights used), not just city.
* Pop by cost as usual, but allow re-expanding a city if this route reaches
* it with strictly fewer flights than any route seen before.
public static int findCheapestPriceDijkstra(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
for (int[] flight : flights) adj.get(flight[0]).add(new int[]{flight[1], flight[2]});

complexity.time: O(k * E) for the Bellman-Ford version — k + 1 rounds over every flight

commonMistakes: Running plain Dijkstra keyed on city alone. It settles a city at its globally cheapest price, which may use more than k stops, and then never reconsiders it — a wrong answer with no warning.
Relaxing in place instead of into a cloned array. Within one round, a flight relaxed after another can chain onto it, so the result quietly uses more flights than the budget allows.
Using k rounds instead of k + 1. k stops means k + 1 flights; off by one here loses exactly the longest legal route.
Adding to Integer.MAX_VALUE when a city is still unreachable, which overflows to a negative cost that then looks like a bargain.
In the Dijkstra variant, guarding with a plain visited set. The guard must be on the fewest flights used to reach the city, since a pricier but shorter-hop route can still be the answer.
Assuming the answer equals the unconstrained shortest path when k is large. It does once k >= n - 1, but not before.
